name: Bianca Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you do at the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, 58, and I run a slitter that cuts wide rolls of packaging film into narrower rolls. I've got a vocational machine-operations certificate and twelve years on this line. I can set the knives and judge a wandering edge, though a specialist repairs the drive when it fails.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your finances and your habits with AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Elise dispatches buses and our grown children have moved out. My wage is ordinary for an operator, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some other packaging plants within a reasonable journey. I use AI every day to compare material specifications and tidy my defect notes, but I check the roll with a gauge. I like trying new controls early, and I want union rules so every shift gets paid practice and safe staffing. Retirement is a possibility, not a figure we've balanced against our costs yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the slitter crew that AI might write cleaner orders for film, but the edge still has to wind straight. I would ask for the new material specification before changing a knife setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages and four months saved cover the regular bills. Office planning alone leaves the physical slitter running and does not put my shift in immediate danger. I still want the person on the other end of the roll to flag a bad wind, whatever the order sheet says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue setting knives, checking the edge with a gauge, and using my usual daily AI search for specifications. I would bring the new order sheet to the monthly union safety meeting to ask whether line speed or staffing has changed; I would save a little new wage money after each full paid month if our bills allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my hours today. A shiny specification is useful only if the film roll passes the gauge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the bad wind show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The edge steps outward halfway through the roll, so the next machine cannot feed it cleanly. I stop the slitter, measure the width, and reset the guide before we make more scrap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring an office order sheet to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the material or line speed changes, the person catching the roll needs time to inspect it. At the next meeting I would ask the delegate to get the speed and staffing written down.

say: A cleaner **film order** still needs a straight physical winding edge.
I would take any changed **speed target** to the union meeting.
think: Current **operator pay** and four months saved cover ordinary bills.
Office planning leaves my **slitter shift** needed for now.
do: **Keep** setting knives and gauging the wound film edge.
**Ask** the union delegate for written speed and staffing changes.
**Save** new full-month wages after bills when a surplus exists.
feel: **Calm** while the physical slitter and current paid shifts remain needed.
S0.quote: A shiny specification is useful only if the film roll passes the gauge.
fieldNote: Her **experienced mid-level work** includes knife settings and gauge checks, with drive repairs referred to a specialist.
Her **daily AI use** is existing specification research; any savings are new additions from paid wages after bills.

steps.text: Keep setting slitter knives and gauging wound film
Ask delegate at monthly union meeting for written speed and staffing changes
Save new wages after full paid months if bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can reorder film before a capable robot can change a heavy roll. I would offer to test a guarded edge camera, but I want the proposed paid roster beside the test sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am curious about the camera, yet management might join shifts if it reduces scrap and take away some of my ordinary wage. Elise's steady dispatcher pay and four months saved give us a little room, not an open-ended replacement. The test must prove it sees a wandering edge before anyone removes the catcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a paid supervised trial with guards in place and compare the proposed roster to my last four wage slips. If the trial is offered, I would learn the new AI edge-alert screen using good and miswound scrap rolls, checking every alert with a gauge beside the setter. If paid hours actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe local packaging jobs whose base wage after travel and shift hours cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible paid-hour loss, while genuinely interested in the camera. I want the wage calculation on the same table as the trial results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a camera trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark a roll that drifts by a few millimetres and one that stays within tolerance. The setter and I would compare the camera alerts with the gauge, with the blade stopped for adjustments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any local plant pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a few, but I would need an actual posting with the base rate, journey and shift pattern. I would not trade a known wage for an advertised bonus that depends on overtime.

say: A guarded **edge-camera trial** should accompany the proposed roster.
I would compare AI alerts with **gauge readings** before trusting them.
think: Merged **paid shifts** could reduce my ordinary operator wage.
Elise's pay and four months **saved** allow only limited adjustment.
do: **Request** a paid guarded camera trial and compare four wage slips.
**Learn** AI edge alerts only if supervised scrap-roll practice is offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local packaging at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible hours loss despite interest in the new display.
S1.quote: I want the wage calculation on the same table as the trial results.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** is conditional practical edge-alert work on a paid guarded trial, beyond daily specification searches.
A **job application** follows actual hours lost and requires a posted safe local role at enough base pay after travel.

steps.text: Request paid guarded camera trial and compare proposed roster with pay slips
Learn AI edge alerts if supervised scrap-roll practice is offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe local packaging if net base pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that AGI could plan film orders in 2028, while capable robots to load rolls and set knives arrive around 2031. The plant should negotiate paid places before ordering that robot slitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots reach the hands-on work. I expect several slitter shifts, perhaps mine, to disappear; four months saved and Elise's pay would help, but losing my full wage would force painful cuts. I have been waking up wondering how long the rent would fit on one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone the planned new sofa and keep the money for housing costs. I would attend the union branch's next bargaining meeting to press for funded paid training and safe line staffing. I would enrol in a locally accepted film-quality certificate only if a place covers fees, paid release and supervised guarded slitter practice. After qualifying and losing hours, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if base pay after travel and shifts covers our bills; without a course place, I would search posted safe packaging-machine work on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the prospect of losing most of my paid week. A four-month cushion is a pause button, not another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that course teach on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure film width, document a wandering edge and isolate the knives before a roll change. A trainer should watch those steps behind the guard; I will not claim a quality qualification from videos alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and Elise's dependable pay cover housing, food and health costs. We have not checked that total, so I would search for paid work rather than assume an age supplies it.

say: The **2028 planning AGI** arrives before physical slitter robots around 2031.
Our **union branch** should bargain for paid places before installation.
think: At **63**, losing most slitter shifts could remove my main wage.
Four months **saved** gives a search window, not permanent household support.
do: **Postpone** the sofa purchase and hold cash for housing.
**Attend** the union bargaining meeting to seek funded paid safe places.
**Enrol** in accepted guarded quality training, then apply to posted local jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and waking over rent.
S2.quote: A four-month cushion is a pause button, not another wage.
fieldNote: Her **2031 fear** concerns physical robots loading and cutting film after 2028 AGI changes order planning.
Both **quality and fallback work** need actual safe local postings with wages after travel and shifts that cover costs.

steps.text: Postpone planned sofa and retain cash for housing
Attend union bargaining meeting for funded paid safe training and staffing
Enrol in accepted quality certificate only if funded paid guarded practice offered
Apply after cuts to posted local quality if qualified or packaging otherwise at viable net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan film orders in 2031 and capable robots might handle the slitter around 2034. Five years lets us demand a real paid course schedule and test whether local plants want its certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. Elise and I might choose retirement by then, but only if written income after housing and health costs supports us; four months saved does not answer that. I like learning early, yet an unrecognised badge would waste time we could spend earning wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add new money from full paid months to our reserve after bills, and ask the union branch at its scheduled meeting to seek paid release for film-quality training. I would enrol only if local job postings accept the certificate and a funded place includes supervised guarded knife isolation. If shifts fall after I qualify, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs whose guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers costs; if no course opens, I would apply to posted safe packaging-machine jobs on those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether a later job will pay enough, but five years gives us time to compare real offers. A factory transition plan should not rely on my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a certificate is recognised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its title with two current local quality postings and ask the hiring offices whether the guarded practice counts. If neither accepts it, I would ask the union for another funded option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you add to savings even with four months already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, from new full-month wages after our rent, food and travel. The existing four months stays an existing cushion; I am talking about an additional amount.

Local **quality postings** should confirm an accepted certificate.
think: At **66**, retirement still depends on written income after costs.
An **unrecognised badge** would cost wages without opening a job.
do: **Save** new full-month wages after household bills.
**Enrol** only if a locally accepted funded paid guarded quality place opens.

S3.quote: A factory transition plan should not rely on my partner's wage.

steps.text: Save new full-month wages after rent food and travel
Ask union branch at scheduled meeting for paid quality-course release
Enrol only if accepted funded paid guarded slitter course offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop AGI could plan film orders in 2036, while capable robots might load the slitter around 2039. A decade gives us time to sort retirement figures, if the plant keeps paying for the work in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those robots arrive, if I am still on shift. Elise and I may be able to stop earlier, but written retirement income must cover housing, food and health costs first. Our regular pay and four-month reserve make this year manageable, though the later calculation is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid slitter shifts and request written retirement-income estimates and a household cost list this year. If I still need work, I would enrol in an accepted film-quality course only with funded fees, paid release and supervised guarded practice. If I remain employed after 2036 and paid hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local packaging or quality jobs whose guaranteed pay after travel and shifts covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant choice, not frightened about this month's rent. I would rather check the figures with Elise than let a date make the choice for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make stopping work possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elise and I would compare written income with rent, food, transport and likely health costs. If the reliable total covers them, I would stop before a robot forced the issue; otherwise I would keep seeking paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no funded course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the safe slitter shifts while offered and look at actual posted packaging roles if hours fall. I would not pay for an unaccepted course while the plant keeps the training budget.

say: I would separate **2036 order AGI** from physical slitter robots around 2039.
Written **retirement figures** should guide any earlier exit.
think: At **71**, I might have stopped only if reliable income covers costs.
Regular **current pay** and four months saved secure near-term bills.
do: **Keep** safe paid slitter shifts and request written retirement figures.
**Enrol** only in accepted funded paid guarded quality training if still needed.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe jobs at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about later retirement sums while present bills remain manageable.
S4.quote: Our regular pay and four-month reserve make this year manageable, though the later calculation is open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture is hardest because the physical slitter shifts could disappear before our retirement income is known. Written staffing dates, a paid guarded quality course local plants recognise, and posted safe jobs at enough guaranteed pay after travel would help. I would want the union at the table before the robot order is signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who carries the roll away when the test camera rejects it. The people handling scrap need a paid place in the new plan too.

headlineQuote: The people handling scrap need a paid place in the new plan too.
portrait: **Bianca**, 58, is an experienced mid-level packaging-film slitter operator with a vocational certificate and average trade skill.
She and her **partner Elise** have grown children, typical operator pay, four months of expenses saved and some packaging plants nearby.
She uses **AI daily** for specifications, checks film physically and supports union bargaining for paid safe training on every shift.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten her wage; an earlier retirement choice needs written income that covers real costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 slitter robots** could remove her paid physical shifts before a viable job or affordable retirement is established.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded training on paid time and posted safe local jobs with workable wages after travel.
